title: The Poisson Approximation to the Binomial
short: When n is large and p is small, Binomial(n, p) is close to Poisson with λ = np.
trouble: Students use the approximation when p is not small, where it can be far off.

blocks.html: A binomial distribution with many trials and a small chance on each, such as defects in a day's production, is tedious to compute exactly. The Poisson distribution is its limit, and a very good approximation.
If $n$ is large, $p$ is small and $\lambda = np$ is moderate, then $$\binom{n}{k}p^{k}(1 - p)^{n - k} \approx e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^{k}}{k!}.$$

Put $p = \frac{\lambda}{n}$ and let $n$ grow with $k$ fixed: $$\binom{n}{k}\left(\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{k}\left(1 - \frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{n - k} = \frac{\lambda^{k}}{k!} \cdot \frac{n(n - 1)\cdots(n - k + 1)}{n^{k}} \cdot \left(1 - \frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{n}\left(1 - \frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{-k}.$$ The second factor tends to 1, the third to $e^{-\lambda}$ (the limit from calculus), and the last to 1. What is left is the Poisson pmf. This is also why Poisson counts arise: split time into many tiny slots, each with a tiny chance of an event.

The slot picture is worth keeping. A window holds a huge number of tiny moments, each with a tiny, independent chance of an event; the binomial count over those moments is essentially Poisson. The same picture, run through time, becomes the Poisson process later in this course.

blocks.name: prob-poisson
blocks.cap: One window cut into slots, each with chance 3 divided by the number of slots of holding an arrival. With more slots, the binomial bars match the Poisson bars.

blocks.title: Defective chips
blocks.q: A factory makes 500 chips a day, each defective with probability $0.004$, independently. Approximate the probability of no defective chips.

blocks.title: When it fails
steps: The binomial's variance is $np(1 - p) = 5$, while the Poisson's is 10: the shapes differ.

blocks.html: A common rule of thumb: the approximation is good when $n \ge 100$ and $np \le 10$, or more loosely when $p \le 0.05$. The error is roughly of size $p$, so the smaller $p$ is, the better. For quick work, $P(\text{no events}) = (1 - p)^{n} \approx e^{-np}$ is the most used case.

Using the approximation when $p$ is not small. The Poisson has variance equal to its mean; a binomial has variance $np(1 - p)$, which is close to $np$ only when $p$ is near 0. Check: is $p$ below about $0.05$ with $n$ in the hundreds? If not, compute the binomial exactly or use a normal approximation.
